newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE - Hidden Ireland fights back against drugs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hidden Ireland fights back against drugs.

text.p: Snow dusts the Wicklow hills beneath a pale winter sun; the wooded glens on the outskirts of Dublin are a Christmas card scene.
A sign welcomes tourists to "The Garden of Ireland." Since 1994 they have regularly outnumbered the country's 3.5 million population, drawn by an image of an unspoilt, pleasant land.
But on the other side of the hills, where Dublin's fair city peters out into satellite suburbs, lies a hidden Ireland the guide books do not prepare them for.
This is Tallaght. Row after row of identical 1960s houses and little else. It is a bleak place, literally and metaphorically on the fringes of modern, thriving Ireland.
And it is on the front line of a people's war against drugs. Driven by fear, terrorised by the thieving of addicts desperate for cash for their next fix, the community is fighting back.
This is one of the places where so-called Drugs Vigilantes set themselves up to hound pushers from the community and addicts into care. It is a war they think they are winning.

Worried parents nightly man "Drug Huts" standing by braziers and chase pushers from the area. They have, by their own account, forced them to flee their 50 Irish pound ($90) a month subsidised council homes.
POPULAR ANGER AT DRUGS MENACE

"Pushers out," says the new graffiti. It is a scene being replicated in housing estates across Ireland in an unprecedented show of popular anger at a menace which has created 10,000 addicts in Dublin alone and sullied the country's image.
"Crime has fallen by 14 percent here since the anti-drugs movement swung into gear," said Conor Lenihan, who will run for the opposition Fianna Fail party at the next election.

Law and order is also expected to be a battle ground when Fianna Fail leads the charge to oust Prime Minister John Bruton's left-right coalition. Already the party is campaigning that it will "put criminals where they belong, behind bars."

The election is due by November next year, but many politicians expect it early in 1997 after a January budget which will feature big tax cuts to reward wage earners who have helped Ireland towards one of Europe's strongest economic growth rates.
"Ireland has no problem generating wealth," said Lenihan. "But look around you. It has major problems distributing it. Unemployment on this estate is between 70 and 90 percent."

A few minutes' drive away is a nondescript set of traffic lights which proved a crossroads in the nations' approach to drugs. Here one June morning, a suspected "hit man" shot dead Veronica Guerin, Ireland's top investigative reporter.
It is an unsolved murder but police believe a gangland drug baron was responsible. Her death prompted a government crackdown on crime which it will defend when the election comes.
CRACKDOWN ON CRIME
Money has been found to build more jails; a unit has been set up to confiscate the assets of organised crime; the law is to be changed to deny bail to people who might re-offend.
But the electioneering goes over the head of Tallaght's 100,000 people. They have taken the law into their own hands, and it feels good.

"This was a pretty place 16 years ago, with the hills behind and trees everywhere. But the drugs came in the 90s and our lives went downhill. Buses won't stop here because they fear they will get robbed by some junkie," says Leslie.
"Look at it. No playgrounds, no shops, no buses, no services, no cars because people fear they'll be robbed. I've one son in prison - he's a junkie too," says Anne.
The Vigilante movement has aroused mixed feelings in the nation's 10,000-strong police. Tales of people being physically intimdated or molested sit uneasily with the force.
"Has summary justice ever led to a stable society ?," asked Police Commissioner Patrick Byrne in a speech last month.
RENEWED SENSE OF COMMUNITY

The people of Tallaght argue that it has, and a new-found sense of community too in which the victims of the drugs craze are being treated by a locally-based system which the government is studying as a model for other places.
"I'm looking after 20 robbers," joked Liam Collins, who supervises a project which dispenses the heroin substitute methadone to addicts and steers them back towards self-respect.

In the past addicts had to go to Dublin to get mathadone. But Collins has found a doctor who will come to Tallaght, a trip few in the medical profession would make because of its reputation for crime and drugs.
"We have a 75 percent success rate. I can remember when the streets of this estate were strewn with discarded syringes. You won't find that now," he added.
His base is a draughty community hall protected by iron railings. Here his charges play pool, talk in group therapy, share the pain and pleasures of detoxification.
Tony, 27, is one. "I started taking drugs when I was 17. I took stuff that they give cancer patients to ease the pain. When I couldn't get that, I moved onto heroin," he said.
He is calm but edgy, only eight months out of a habit which cost him between 10 and 300 pounds a day ($16 and $480) on an income of unemployment benefit of 65 ($104) a week.
"This is the longest I've been out of prison. Every day I used to get up and think about what I was gonna rob to get the gear (drugs). Now I don't have to. I'm back in control."
